lines.text: A row's own version chain holds two things right now: an old version that already committed, and a brand-new version a transaction just wrote but hasn't committed yet.
An existing reader already took its own snapshot earlier. Which one of those two versions does that reader actually see?
The old, committed one.
Until that newer transaction actually commits, its version simply isn't visible to anyone else yet.
Run it for real: the reader's own snapshot genuinely returned the old value, even while the chain's own newest entry already held the new one.
So which version a reader sees depends on that version's own metadata together with the snapshot, never simply on which one happens to be newest.
That same newer transaction now goes ahead and commits.
Does the original reader's own snapshot change what it reports, now that the write behind it is finally committed?
No, it doesn't change at all.
It keeps reporting exactly what it reported before.
Run it for real: the original reader's own snapshot kept returning exactly the same value after that commit as it did before it.
A transaction now updates a row it's able to see.
Does that update ever rewrite the existing version's own stored fields directly, in place?
No, never.
A brand-new version gets appended instead, and only the old version's own deleting-transaction marker gets stamped.
Run it for real: the superseded version's own fields came back completely untouched afterward, and the chain genuinely grew by exactly one brand-new entry.
One real production system states this exact guarantee directly, in its own documentation.
Does that system ever let a long write force a concurrent read to wait, or the other way around, a long read forcing a write to wait?

lines.text: Neither one, genuinely.
Reading never blocks writing there, and writing never blocks reading either.
That system's own documentation states it in exactly those words: reading never blocks writing, and writing never blocks reading.
That same system's own documentation also names exactly what this topic's own version metadata has been standing in for all along.

Its own version-identity column records the inserting transaction for a row version, and its own deletion-identity column records the deleting transaction, or stays at zero while a version is still undeleted.

So here's the shape of this whole topic: which single version of a row a reader gets to see depends on that version's own metadata together with the reader's own fixed snapshot, never simply on which version happens to be newest.
A writer never rewrites an existing version in place; it appends a brand-new one instead, and leaves the old one's own fields exactly as they were.
That one choice is the entire reason a real production system can promise what it promises: a long write never forces a read to wait, and a long read never forces a write to wait either.
